[PAPER_0068, relevance_score=0.271] Study 6

In Studies 6a and 6b, we tested the underlying assumption that zero-sum configurations of success increase perceptions of hostility compared to non-zero-sum configurations of success. While previous research has found that competitive situations lead to lower attributions of warmth compared to cooperative situations (Caprariello et al., 2009; Fiske, 2018), here, we hypothesized that even in the same competitive settings with the same rewards, a zero-sum configuration of those rewards promotes hostile attributions.

[PAPER_0070, relevance_score=0.282] Meanwhile, those high in zero-sum mindset will respond as if in a zero-sum situation-demonstrating stronger hostile attribution bias and greater intention to "retaliate," a potential behavioral implication of hostile attribution bias (Crick & Dodge, 1996; Dodge, 2006; Klein Tuente et al., 2019)-even in objectively non-zero-sum situations.

Hypothesis 6a: Zero-sum configurations of success increase hostile attributions.

Hypothesis 6b: Zero-sum mindset predicts hostile attributions across situations, including in objectively non-zero-sum situations.
items.paper_content_summary: Study 6 predicted greater hostile attribution in zero-sum situations, and stronger hostile attribution and retaliation intentions among people with stronger zero-sum mindsets. It also predicted weaker responsiveness to the objective situation at stronger mindsets and explored mindset-related situational beliefs, including in non-zero-sum situations. [PREREG_0001, relevance_score=0.327] Title: Zero-Sum Mindset and Hostile Attributions in Zero-Sum and Non-Zero-Sum Situations - A Pre-Registered Replication

Description: This is a pre-registered replication of an earlier study examining the effect of zero-sum (vs. non-zero-sum) configurations of success on hostile attributions in competitive situations. This study also adds manipulation checks of zero-sum beliefs about the situations.

q2: Hypothesis 1: Zero-sum configurations of success promote hostile attributions.

[PREREG_0002, relevance_score=0.342] That is, when competitive situations are structured as zero-sum, individuals are more likely to attribute hostile intent to other competitors than when competitive situations are structured as non-zero-sum. (i.e., main effect of zero-sum situation on hostile attributions)

Hypothesis 2: Zero-sum mindset predicts stronger hostile attributions (even in objectively non-zero-sum situations).

[PREREG_0003, relevance_score=0.333] That is, across competitive situations, individuals who hold a stronger zero-sum mindset are more likely to attribute hostile intent to other competitors than individuals who hold a weaker/non-zero-sum mindset (i.e., main effect of zero-sum mindset on hostile attributions).

Hypothesis 3: Zero-sum mindset predicts greater intention to retaliate against the perceived hostility across situations, including in objectively non-zero-sum situations.

[PREREG_0004, relevance_score=0.359] That is, across competitive situations, individuals who hold a stronger zero-sum mindset are more likely to intend to retaliate against other competitors than individuals who hold a weaker/non-zero-sum mindset (i.e., main effect of zero-sum mindset on retaliation intentions).

q3: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.

q4: For studies that involve human subjects, they will not know the treatment group to which they have been assigned.

[PREREG_0021, relevance_score=0.380] q16.question: Likert-style scales will be computed as mean scores for all scales (with reverse-key items reverse-coded). See analysis plan and markdown attached for all steps taken to compute indices.

q17.question: Before we test our main hypotheses, we will first examine whether the scenarios describing zero-sum competitions do actually promote zero-sum beliefs about those competitive situations (manipulation check) by comparing mean zero-sum belief ratings. Comparing these means in an independent samples t-test, we expect to find stronger zero-sum beliefs in the zero-sum condition than in the non-zero-sum condition.

[PREREG_0022, relevance_score=0.435] Next we test our main hypotheses. Hypothesis 1: Zero-sum configurations of success increase hostile attributions. We test this hypothesis using an independent samples t-test comparing mean levels of hostile attribution bias between conditions (expecting higher mean hostile attributions in the zero-sum condition). Hypothesis 2: Zero-sum mindset predicts stronger hostile attributions (even in objectively non-zero-sum situations). We primarily test this hypothesis using multiple regression analyses to predict hostile attribution bias from zero-sum mindset when controlling for the effect of condition.

[PREREG_0023, relevance_score=0.389] We hypothesize that stronger zero-sum mindset will predict stronger hostile attribution bias even when controlling for the effect of the objective situations (i.e., the experimental condition). As a secondary test of this hypothesis, we will also examine whether zero-sum mindset moderates the effect of the "objective situation" on hostile attributions by examining the interaction of zero-sum mindset and condition.

[PREREG_0024, relevance_score=0.319] We predict that when zero-sum mindset is stronger, the effect of the "objective situation" (i.e., the expected negative effect of a non-zero-sum configurations on hostile attributions) will be weaker (i.e., a negative interaction term coefficient when zero-sum condition is the reference level).

[PREREG_0025, relevance_score=0.455] However, we also note that the effect-size of this moderation observed in an earlier study was relatively small compared to the main effect of zero-sum mindset and main effect of condition on hostile attributions, and therefore, may require a larger sample size than that which is available for this study to detect at the power and significance thresholds applied to our main hypothesis tests. Given these constraints and the directional nature of the hypothesis, this secondary hypothesis will be tested using a one-tailed test.

[PREREG_0033, relevance_score=0.431] Therefore, we will examine whether zero-sum mindset predicts situationally-specific zero-sum beliefs in two ways: By examining only participants in the non-zero-sum condition, we examine whether a stronger zero-sum mindset will predict stronger situationally-specific zero-sum beliefs. And in the full sample, we examine the interaction between zero-sum mindset and condition predicting situationally-specific zero-sum beliefs.

Note: This hypothesis is exploratory because a significant relationship between zero-sum mindset and the manipulation check variable is not essential to the main hypothesis that zero-sum mindset predicts hostile attributions (even in non-zero-sum situations).

Procedure and Materials

Experimental Set-Up

Participants were presented with four vignettes (modeled after Dodge et al., 2015) describing four different kinds of competitive situations: athletics, academics, politics, and the job market (Figure 2 illustrates the experiment flow with examples from the job market vignette).

2

[PAPER_0080, relevance_score=0.299] Study 6a Experimental Flow

For each domain, participants read vignettes describing the competitive situation, the reward structure (zero-sum or non-zero-sum), and an ambiguous incident. Importantly, the competitive contexts (e.g., running a race, interviewing for a job) and the objective outcomes of success (e.g., qualifying for the next race, getting the job), and the ambiguous situations (e.g., someone tosses a cup that you trip on, someone spills coffee on your shirt) were the same in both conditions.

[PAPER_0081, relevance_score=0.328] The only thing that varied between the experimental conditions was the description of the reward structure, that is, whether success is zero-sum (e.g., only the first few across the finish line will qualify, only one job available) or non-zero-sum (e.g., qualification based on race finish time, variable number of job positions to be filled by qualified candidates). After reading each vignette, participants rated their perceptions of hostility and their intention to retaliate.

[PAPER_0082, relevance_score=0.341] After completing all measures in the experimental conditions, participants also completed measures of zero-sum mindset and demographic variables (age, sex, race, education, income). In the preregistered replication (Study 6b), we also included manipulation check questions immediately following the situation descriptions (and preceding the ambiguous situations) to measure the extent to which people did, in fact, perceive the situations as zero-sum (or not).

q17.question: Before we test our main hypotheses, we will first examine whether the scenarios describing zero-sum competitions do actually promote zero-sum beliefs about those competitive situations (manipulation check) by comparing mean zero-sum belief ratings. Comparing these means in an independent samples t-test, we expect to find stronger zero-sum beliefs in the zero-sum condition than in the non-zero-sum condition.

[PREREG_0022, relevance_score=0.341] Next we test our main hypotheses. Hypothesis 1: Zero-sum configurations of success increase hostile attributions. We test this hypothesis using an independent samples t-test comparing mean levels of hostile attribution bias between conditions (expecting higher mean hostile attributions in the zero-sum condition). Hypothesis 2: Zero-sum mindset predicts stronger hostile attributions (even in objectively non-zero-sum situations). We primarily test this hypothesis using multiple regression analyses to predict hostile attribution bias from zero-sum mindset when controlling for the effect of condition.

[PREREG_0023, relevance_score=0.286] We hypothesize that stronger zero-sum mindset will predict stronger hostile attribution bias even when controlling for the effect of the objective situations (i.e., the experimental condition). As a secondary test of this hypothesis, we will also examine whether zero-sum mindset moderates the effect of the "objective situation" on hostile attributions by examining the interaction of zero-sum mindset and condition.

[PREREG_0025, relevance_score=0.353] However, we also note that the effect-size of this moderation observed in an earlier study was relatively small compared to the main effect of zero-sum mindset and main effect of condition on hostile attributions, and therefore, may require a larger sample size than that which is available for this study to detect at the power and significance thresholds applied to our main hypothesis tests. Given these constraints and the directional nature of the hypothesis, this secondary hypothesis will be tested using a one-tailed test.

[PREREG_0026, relevance_score=0.320] Hypothesis 3: Zero-sum mindset predicts greater intention to retaliate against the perceived hostility across situations, including in objectively non-zero-sum situations. We test this hypothesis using multiple regression analyses to predict retaliation intentions from zero-sum mindset when controlling for the effect of condition. We hypothesize that a stronger zero-sum mindset will predict stronger hostile attribution bias even when controlling for the effect of the objective situations (i.e., the experimental condition).
